title: Untitled
description: Untitled , circa 1977 signed 'J. Mitchell' (lower right) watercolor, pastel and crayon on paper 14 3/8 x 9 1/4 in. 36.5 x 23.5 cm.
provenance: Jean Lamouroux, France (acquired directly from the artist) | Robert Miller Gallery, New York | Acquired directly from the above by the present owner in 2002 | | Exhibited | Boulder, CU Art Museum, University of Colorado Boulder, Points of View: Selections from Seven Colorado Collections, 8 September-17 December 2011, exh. cat., p. 52, illustrated in color | | Throughout her decades-long career, Joan Mitchell's visionary approach to painting, drawing, and printmaking continually resulted in emotionally invigorated images inspired by memories of nature, people, music and writing. The present lot is no exception. Bursting on the paper with an array of harmonious and assertive colors and lines, Mitchell's poetic and instinctual relationship to her creative practice is palpable in this Untitled piece from the late 1970s, a period in which the artist was at the apex of her practice. Harnessing the creative force of emotions, Mitchell honors the intimacy and profundity of the human psyche. In Untitled, Mitchell translates the intangible into an astute yet uninhibited composition in a symphony of color that embodies the artist's singularity within Abstract Expressionism. Working across differing scales throughout her career, the present lot further demonstrates Mitchell's conscious approach to drawing in which the surface area acts as the perfectly sized stage on which the gestural strokes dance across the sheet. An icon of her era, Mitchell's resonant impact on the Post-War period remains indelible and deeply influential to generations of artists.

title: An Ounce of Luck
description: An Ounce of Luck , 1989 signed 'Ernie Barnes' (lower right) acrylic on canvas 20 x 24 in. 50.8 x 61 cm. This work is included in the forthcoming Ernie Barnes Catalogue Raisonné. We would like to thank Luz Rodriguez for her assistance in cataloguing this work. The copyright to this painting is reserved by © Ernie Barnes.
provenance: Private Collection, New Hampshire (acquired from the artist in 1989) | | Literature | W. Lowe, Jr., 'An Ounce of Luck,' Playboy Magazine, September 1989, vol. 36, no. 9, pp. 80-81, illustrated | | Universally known for the title image for the classic sitcom "Good Times" (1974-1979); the cover of Marvin Gaye's 1976 album "I Want You", and The Crusaders 1984 album "Ghetto Blaster," Ernie Barnes' significance as a cultural icon of late 20th century America is an established fact. His life and art have been the subject of retrospectives at the California African American Museum in summer 2019, and a recent New York Times piece described his canvases as "domains of earnestness and striving, of unalloyed celebration and pride", and Barnes himself "an artist of the people – most especially of Black people" (Adam Bradley, 'Millions Saw His Paintings on TV. In the Art World, His Work Still Went Unnoticed', The New York Times, 15 September 2023, Online). His impact and the beauty of his paintings cannot be divided from his legacy as a champion of the Black experience and the American history of 20th century painting. | | Ernie Barnes' signature style is well illustrated in An Ounce of Luck while also framing the structure of Lowe's story. The tall, lean figures of the main characters dominate the foreground, and in this positioning, Barnes highlights clearly their differences in disposition. His stylized approach to the human form is on full display in An Ounce of Luck, as is his talent for small details that create the compelling narrative. The musculature in the figures' necks, the stylized feet and arms exemplify Barnes' classic depictions of athletes. A virtuosic display of Barnes' talent, it is a splendid and prominently published example by one of the great painters of the 20th century.

title: Mujer con Vasija
description: Mujer con Vasija , 1976 signed and dated 'Ricardo Martínez 76' (lower right) signed again, titled and dated again ''""MUJER CON VASIJA" 1976 Ricardo Martínez' (on the stretcher) oil on canvas 39 3/4 x 58 1/2 in. 101 x 148.6 cm. We would like to thank the Fundación Ricardo Martíne z for their assistance in cataloguing and confirming the authenticity of this work which is registered under archive number FRM000939.
provenance: Collection of Paul and Gwenda Klein, Los Altos, CA | Rubicon Gallery, Los Altos, CA | Estate of Douglas Watson, Los Angeles | Acquired directly from the above by the present owner in March 1996 | | Literature | Luis Cardoza y Aragón, Ricardo Martínez, México: Joaquín Mortiz, 1981, no. 86, illustrated | | In Ricardo Martínez's monumental masterpiece Mujer con Vasija (1976), a massive, primordial female figure gazes into a warm, golden glow, her form blending seamlessly with the surrounding darkness. This powerful symbol of fertility tenderly offers a vessel as a tribute or celebration to someone or something beyond the canvas, hidden from the viewer's sight. Mujer con Vasija represents a transformative moment in Martínez's artistic journey, a significant shift that marked the development of his mature style. Consistent expressions, a distinct visual language, and a sense of universality characterize this stage in his practice. | | Martínez's early works reflect the influence of Julio Castellanos, and later, he was inspired by Federico Cantu, with whom he formed a friendship in 1943. Over time, the stylistic influences of Manuel Rodriguez Lozano, José Clemente Orozco, and Giorgio de Chirico emerged in his art. | | It wasn't until 1953 that Martínez's style underwent a definitive transformation. Like many artists of his era, he became captivated by pre-Hispanic art, which profoundly influenced his work moving forward. His works from 1953 to 1957 marked a shift toward the style for which he would become known, incorporating shapes and features inspired by pre-Hispanic sculptures and masks. This period allowed him to establish a unique visual language that would define his artistic output for the rest of his life, deeply rooted in his cultural heritage. | | During this time, his "costumbrista paintings" depicted Indian peasants engaged in traditional activities, showcasing their daily lives and cultural elements—such as music and food—set against vibrant backgrounds, reminiscent of the scene in Los Elotes from 1954. These 'costumbrista paintings' were significant in Martínez's oeuvre. They marked a departure from his earlier influences and a move towards a more unique and personal expression, setting the stage for his later, more mature works. | | The blurring technique became essential in defining both the contours of the figures and the application of light and color. His mastery in managing light and volume, achieved through color, created a unique atmosphere in his works. The monumentality of the figures, which often dominate the canvas, is matched only by the profound sense of spirituality and deep emotional resonance imbued in each figure, rendering the works and subjects timeless. |

title: Lessender Man (Reading Man)
material: polyester, fiberglass, oil, mixed media, accessories
description: Lessender Man (Reading Man) , 1972 polyester and fiberglass, polychromed in oil, mixed media, with accessories 64 1/2 x 21 x 24 in. 163.8 x 53.3 x 61 cm.
provenance: Mr. and Mrs. George Meeker, Kansas City, MO | Morgan Gallery, Kansas City, MO | Frumkin & Struve Gallery, Chicago | Acquired directly from the above by the present owner in 1988 | | Exhibited | Chicago, Struve Gallery, 1988 | New York, Whitney Museum of American Art at Philip Morris, Urban Figures, 17 November 1988-15 February 1989 | Cologne, Germany, Onnasch Galerie, Duane Hanson, 1972, exh. cat., pp. 7, 11-12, illustrated (different wig) | Stuttgart, Germany, Württembergischer Kunstverein Stuttgart, Duane Hanson, 1974, exh. cat., no. 28, p. 67, illustrated (different wig) | | Literature | Kirk Varnedoe, Duane Hanson, New York: Harry N. Abrams, Inc., Publishers, 1985, pp. 52-53, illustrated in color | Thomas Buchsteiner and Otto Letze, eds., Duane Hanson: Sculptures of the American Dream, Ostfildern-Ruit: Hatje Cantz, 2007, no. 29, p. 45, illustrated in color | Martin H. Bush, Duane Hanson, Edwin A. Ulrich Museum of Art, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, 1976, p. 45, illustrated | | The Reading Man is an outstanding example of one of the 20th century's most important hyperrealist artists. This astonishingly detailed sculpture from 1972 marks a significant transition from Hanson's earlier and more confrontational works of the 1960s, which often featured stark scenes of violence and social unrest. These early works were designed to provoke strong emotional responses from viewers, but with The Reading Man, Hanson shifted to addressing broader social issues in a more understated manner. This shift in style allowed Hanson to delve deeper into the societal implications of his work, exploring themes of everyman and the often mundane moments in modern life. | | Meticulously detailed, The Reading Man presents a man in a black sweater, worn corduroy pants, and shoes typical of 1972. He leans against a wall, holding a newspaper loosely in his hands, and looks down, seemingly reading casually. | In this moment Hanson captures a genuine, quotidian scene of modern life. This hyperrealistic portrayal invites viewers to reflect on the human condition and the societal routines that shape daily existence. The Reading Man is a powerful commentary on the ennui and detachment that can be found in the repetitive activities of daily life. | | Hanson's practice combines disarming sculptural realism with pointed social commentary. He selected ordinary, often overlooked individuals. This sentiment is reflected in works like Supermarket Shopper (1970), Woman Eating (1971), and Tourists (1970). Hanson used polyester resin, fiberglass, and Bondo to create these lifelike sculptures, which were always cast from live models, often from the very societal figures he aimed to depict. The figures were then painted to replicate human skin perfectly, with details extending to veins, blemishes, and individual mustache hairs. The sculptures were dressed in clothing sourced from second-hand stores or provided by the models themselves, adding a layer of authenticity. This authenticity is what makes Hanson's work so striking and thought-provoking. | | Hanson's work continues to resonate within contemporary art, influencing his contemporaries and future generations. Serving as mirrors to society, his sculptures often blur the line between art and life. Hansons' work from the 1970s significantly impacted the art world, seen as an extension of the Pop Art movement's examination of everyday life, but with a more direct and unflinching approach. Hanson's ability to evoke empathy and introspection through hyperrealistic representations of ordinary people solidified his status as a pivotal figure in the contemporary art canon. The profound impact of Hanson's work on contemporary art is a testament to its enduring significance and power.

title: Figure on Beam with Wheels
description: Figure on Beam with Wheels , 1992 burlap, resin and wood 83 7/8 x 94 1/2 x 24 3/8 in. 213 x 240 x 62 cm. This work will be included in the forthcoming Magdalena Abakanowicz Catalogue Raisonné being prepared by Dr. Jolanta Gola under number 918. We would like to thank Dr. Jolanta Gola and the Marta Magdalena Abakanowicz-Kosmowska and Jan Kosmowski Foundation for their assistance in cataloging this work.
provenance: The artist | Marlborough Gallery Inc., New York | Dorothy Goldeen Gallery, Los Angeles | Acquired directly from the above by the present owner in 1994 | | Exhibited | Kraków, BWA, Magdalena Abakanowciz, January-February 1993 | New York, Marlborough Gallery Inc., Magdalena Abakanowicz, 30 April-5 June 1993, exh. cat., no. 10, p. 42, illustrated | San Diego, Mandeville Gallery, University of California, San Diego, Magdalena Abakanowicz: Recent Work and Arboreal Architecture, 15 January-17 February 1994 | | Literature | Leah Ollman, "Tame Offering of a Powerful Artist's Work: UC San Diego exhibits only a small sample of the art of Polish sculptor Magdalena Abakanowicz," Los Angeles Times, 22 January 1994 | | Art has an extraordinary ability to mirror the intricacies of the human experience, and few artists have delved into this theme as profoundly as Magdalena Abakanowicz. Celebrated for her groundbreaking sculptures and installations, Abakanowicz's work offers insights into identity, vulnerability, and the collective human condition. Among her many impactful creations, Figure on Beam with Wheels is a masterpiece in her oeuvre and a testament to her remarkable artistic philosophy and vision. | | Abakanowicz's upbringing in Poland during World War II instilled in her a profound sensitivity to humanity's struggles. This formative background shaped her unique perspective, which she expressed through a distinct sculptural language. Her innovative use of materials and figurative forms captured and conveyed a profound understanding of human vulnerability and resilience, offering a beacon of hope in the face of adversity. | | The Figure Beam series from the early 1990s evolved from Abakanowicz's renowned Abakans—a series of large, organic hanging forms created in the 1960s—and the figural Alteration series from the 1970s. The Alteration series marked a significant shift in her work towards depicting the human figure. In this series, she crafted groups of genderless, hunched humanoid figures made from burlap, often hollowed out and missing heads and arms. The Figure Beam series merges the imposing presence of the Abakans with the figural forms and techniques used in the Alteration series. Unlike the hunched and bowed figures from the Alteration series, the figures in the Figure Beam series stand tall and assertive on a wooden beam, symbolizing the resilience and vulnerability of the human spirit—a recurring theme in her work. These headless and armless figures can appear either alone or in pairs. Abakanowicz uses burlap and resin to create a texture that resembles human skin, giving her sculptures a primitive quality. By incorporating burlap—a material traditionally associated with labor and craftsmanship—she symbolizes resilience. The tactile nature of this material invites viewers to engage with the artwork on a sensory level, fostering a deeper connection to the themes being explored. Additionally, she includes wooden beams on wheels for the figures to balance, which may suggest the power humans can derive from nature. Abakanowicz's exploration of individuality versus collectivity makes this series particularly compelling. Each figure possesses a unique posture and form, yet they share a commonality that encourages viewers to reflect on their identities as part of a larger human tapestry. While the figures stand tall and resolute, their hollow interiors symbolize the emptiness that can accompany modern existence, a theme that resonates universally. | | Her work challenges traditional norms and has left a lasting legacy that will continue to inspire future generations, reinforcing the idea that art can touch upon the most profound aspects of the human experience. As we stand before these striking figures, we are invited to witness and participate in the ongoing conversation about what it means to be part of the human experience. This conversation resonates now more than ever, underscoring the enduring relevance of Abakanowicz's work.
